title: THE WARNING I SAW IN THE FOOLISH VIRGINS RUNNING OUT OF OIL
paragraphs: THE WARNING I SAW IN THE FOOLISH VIRGINS RUNNING OUT OF OIL
There is something deeply unsettling about the story Jesus tells in Matthew 25.
Because the foolish virgins were not rebellious people.

They were not mockers.
They were not outsiders.
They were not enemies of the bridegroom.
They were waiting for Him.
And that is what makes the warning so powerful.

All ten virgins had lamps.
All ten expected the bridegroom.
All ten fell asleep during the delay.
At first glance, there was almost no visible difference between them.
But when midnight came… everything changed.
The cry rang out through the darkness:
"Behold, the bridegroom is coming! Go out to meet him!"

Suddenly the lamps were lifted.
The flames were checked.
The moment everyone had been waiting for had finally arrived.
But then the truth appeared.
Five had oil.
Five did not.
And the difference between them was not visible until the moment that mattered most.
That alone should make every believer pause.
Because this parable is not mainly about wicked people missing God.
It is about unprepared people missing the moment.
The foolish virgins had lamps.

They looked ready.
They looked spiritual.
They looked like they belonged in the procession.
But when the midnight moment came, their lamps began to flicker.
Their fire could not survive the hour.
And suddenly the terrifying realization hit them:
Appearance cannot replace preparation.
They ran to buy oil.
But the moment had already arrived.
And when they returned… the door was closed.
Imagine the silence of that moment.
The celebration inside.
The music.
The laughter.
The light.
And outside the door… five people who thought they would be inside.
They knocked.
"Lord, Lord, open to us."
But the answer that came back was chilling:
"Truly I tell you, I do not know you."
Then Jesus ends the story with one sentence that echoes through history:

"Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour."
— Matthew 25:13
This parable is not meant to scare people into panic.
It is meant to wake people up from spiritual complacency.
Because the foolish virgins teach us something that many people ignore:
You can be around spiritual things and still be unprepared.
You can carry a lamp without carrying oil.
You can attend church, hear sermons, sing worship songs, and still neglect the inner life that keeps the fire burning.
The foolish virgins did not fail at midnight.
They failed long before midnight.
They failed in the quiet hours when preparation seemed unnecessary.
That is where most spiritual failures begin.
Not with rebellion.
But with neglect.
Neglected prayer.
Neglected repentance.
Neglected obedience.
Neglected intimacy with God.
And for a while, nothing looks wrong.
The lamp is still in your hand.
But slowly the oil runs out.
Here is the part that should challenge every believer:
When the foolish virgins asked the wise ones for oil, they were told something surprising.
"No… go to those who sell and buy for yourselves."
At first that response seems harsh.
But it reveals something profound.
There are things no one can give you at the last minute.
No one can lend you a life of prayer.
No one can lend you obedience.
No one can lend you spiritual depth.
No one can lend you intimacy with God.
Some things must be cultivated before the moment arrives.
Faith is not built in a crisis.
It is revealed in a crisis.
And the midnight hour simply exposes what has been prepared in the hidden places.
That is the warning I see in the foolish virgins.
Not that people hate God.
But that many people delay their devotion.
They assume there will always be more time.
More time to pray.
More time to grow.
More time to get serious.
But the entire message of the parable is this:
The moment will come suddenly.
And when it does, readiness cannot be rushed.
Oil cannot be manufactured instantly.
Preparation cannot be borrowed.
And the door that was once open… will eventually close.
But there is also a powerful hope hidden inside this warning.
Jesus did not tell this story to condemn people.
He told it to prepare them.
Because the wise virgins were not extraordinary people.
They simply made sure they had oil.
They understood something many people ignore:

The delay is not permission to drift.
The delay is an opportunity to prepare.
Right now, we are living in the waiting.
The bridegroom has not yet appeared.
The midnight cry has not yet sounded.
The door has not yet closed.
Which means something incredibly important:
There is still time to fill your lamp.
Time to deepen your prayer life.
Time to return to God.
Time to renew your faith.
Time to pursue intimacy with the One you are waiting for.
Because when the cry finally comes…
The only thing that will matter is not how close you were to the wedding.
It will be whether your lamp is still burning.
And maybe the question this parable quietly asks every one of us is this:
If the cry came tonight…
Would your lamp still have oil?

Scripture:
"Watch therefore, for you know neither the day nor the hour in which the Son of Man is coming."
— Matthew 25:13
Reflection Question for You
What do you think the “oil” represents most in a believer’s life today — prayer, obedience, intimacy with God, or something else?
